_help: One file per plexus. Each structure: id, level (radix|truncus|divisio|fasciculus|ramus|terminalis), short = label in the schematic (\n = line break), name = full Latin name, answers = accepted answers (first = shown answer, Latin), en = English names (accepted, but the player is asked to say it in Latin), parents = structures it comes from, roots = segments used to trace the fibre pathway, d = SVG path in the 1260x760 schematic, label = {x,y,anchor} or {t,dx,dy,anchor} (t = point along the path, 0..1), lead = draw a thin leader line from the label to the path point at t. diff: 1 beginner, 2 intermediate, 3 advanced.
title: Plexus brachialis
intro: The Plexus brachialis is formed by the Rami anteriores of the spinal nerves C5–T1. It is organised in five levels – Radices, Trunci, Divisiones, Fasciculi and the terminal nerves. Memory hook: Read That Damn Cadaver Book.

landmarks.text:
between M. scalenus anterior
and M. scalenus medius

Axilla – the Fasciculi are named after
their position around the A. axillaris

ramus.label: Collateral branches – drawn thin, in the colour of the level they leave

structures.name: Radix C5 – Ramus anterior nervi spinalis C5
structures.origin: Ramus anterior of the 5th cervical spinal nerve
structures.course: Leaves the Foramen intervertebrale and runs between M. scalenus anterior and M. scalenus medius (Spatium interscalenum). Joins C6 to form the Truncus superior.
facts: Myotome: shoulder abduction (M. deltoideus)
Dermatome: lateral upper arm
Reflex: biceps reflex (C5–C6)
Direct branches: N. dorsalis scapulae, part of N. thoracicus longus
structures.clinical: Root avulsion C5–C6 = upper plexus lesion (Erb–Duchenne).

structures.name: Radix C6 – Ramus anterior nervi spinalis C6
structures.origin: Ramus anterior of the 6th cervical spinal nerve
structures.course: Runs through the Spatium interscalenum and joins C5 to form the Truncus superior.
facts: Myotome: elbow flexion, wrist extension
Dermatome: lateral forearm and thumb
Reflex: brachioradialis reflex (C5–C6)
Gives a twig to the N. thoracicus longus

structures.name: Radix C7 – Ramus anterior nervi spinalis C7
structures.origin: Ramus anterior of the 7th cervical spinal nerve
structures.course: Runs through the Spatium interscalenum and continues alone as the Truncus medius.
facts: Myotome: elbow extension (M. triceps brachii)
Dermatome: middle finger
Reflex: triceps reflex (C7)
Gives a twig to the N. thoracicus longus

structures.name: Radix C8 – Ramus anterior nervi spinalis C8
structures.origin: Ramus anterior of the 8th cervical spinal nerve
structures.course: Runs through the Spatium interscalenum and joins T1 to form the Truncus inferior.
facts: Myotome: finger flexion
Dermatome: little finger and medial hand
structures.clinical: Root lesion C8–T1 = lower plexus lesion (Klumpke).

structures.name: Radix T1 – Ramus anterior nervi spinalis T1
structures.origin: Ramus anterior of the 1st thoracic spinal nerve (its larger upper part; the rest becomes the 1st intercostal nerve)
structures.course: Ascends over the neck of the first rib and joins C8 to form the Truncus inferior, which lies on the first rib behind the A. subclavia.
facts: Myotome: finger abduction/adduction (Mm. interossei)
Dermatome: medial forearm
structures.clinical: Avulsion of T1 near the spinal cord can also interrupt the sympathetic fibres to the head → Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis).

structures.name: Nervus dorsalis scapulae
structures.origin: Radix C5 (posterior aspect, before the trunk forms)
structures.course: Pierces M. scalenus medius and runs deep to M. levator scapulae towards the medial border of the scapula.
facts: Supraclavicular branch – directly from a root

structures.name: Nervus thoracicus longus
structures.origin: Radices C5, C6 and C7 (posterior aspect)
structures.course: Descends behind the plexus and runs on the outer surface of M. serratus anterior along the lateral chest wall (Linea axillaris media).
facts: Supraclavicular branch – directly from the roots
Memory: C5, 6, 7 – "wings of heaven"
structures.clinical: Injury (axillary lymph node dissection, mastectomy, heavy loads on the shoulder) → Scapula alata: the medial border of the scapula lifts off when the patient pushes against a wall; arm elevation above 90° is weak.

structures.name: Truncus superior
structures.origin: Union of the Radices C5 and C6
structures.course: Lies in the Trigonum cervicale laterale (posterior triangle of the neck) above the A. subclavia.
facts: Branches: N. suprascapularis, N. subclavius
Splits into a Divisio anterior and a Divisio posterior
structures.clinical: Upper trunk lesion (Erb–Duchenne palsy) – e.g. birth trauma with shoulder dystocia or a fall that pushes head and shoulder apart: arm hangs adducted and internally rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated ("waiter's tip"). Loss of M. deltoideus, M. supraspinatus, M. infraspinatus, M. biceps brachii, M. brachialis.

structures.name: Truncus medius
structures.origin: Continuation of the Radix C7 alone
structures.course: Lies in the Trigonum cervicale laterale between the upper and lower trunk.
facts: No own branches
Splits into a Divisio anterior and a Divisio posterior

structures.name: Truncus inferior
structures.origin: Union of the Radices C8 and T1
structures.course: Lies on the first rib behind the A. subclavia.
facts: No own branches
Splits into a Divisio anterior and a Divisio posterior
structures.clinical: Lower trunk lesion (Klumpke palsy) – sudden upward pull of the arm, birth with the arm raised, cervical rib or Pancoast tumour: weak intrinsic hand muscles → claw hand; sensory loss on the medial forearm and hand; possible Horner syndrome if T1 is involved.

structures.name: Nervus suprascapularis
structures.course: Passes through the Incisura scapulae below the Lig. transversum scapulae superius (the A. suprascapularis runs above the ligament), then around the neck of the scapula into the Fossa infraspinata.
facts: Also sensory to the shoulder joint and the acromioclavicular joint
Supraclavicular branch
structures.clinical: Entrapment in the Incisura scapulae → weak start of abduction (M. supraspinatus) and weak external rotation (M. infraspinatus), atrophy above and below the Spina scapulae.

structures.name: Nervus subclavius
structures.course: Descends in front of the plexus and the A. subclavia to the M. subclavius below the clavicle.
facts: Often gives a N. phrenicus accessorius
Supraclavicular branch

structures.name: Divisio anterior trunci superioris
structures.course: Behind the clavicle; joins the anterior division of the Truncus medius to form the Fasciculus lateralis.
facts: Anterior divisions carry the fibres for the flexor (anterior) compartments

structures.name: Divisio posterior trunci superioris
structures.course: Behind the clavicle; joins the other two posterior divisions to form the Fasciculus posterior.
facts: Posterior divisions carry the fibres for the extensor (posterior) compartments

structures.name: Divisio anterior trunci medii
structures.course: Behind the clavicle; joins the anterior division of the Truncus superior to form the Fasciculus lateralis.
facts: Anterior divisions carry the fibres for the flexor (anterior) compartments

structures.name: Divisio posterior trunci medii
structures.course: Behind the clavicle; joins the other posterior divisions to form the Fasciculus posterior.
facts: Posterior divisions carry the fibres for the extensor (posterior) compartments

structures.name: Divisio anterior trunci inferioris
structures.course: Behind the clavicle; continues alone as the Fasciculus medialis.
facts: Anterior divisions carry the fibres for the flexor (anterior) compartments

structures.name: Divisio posterior trunci inferioris
structures.course: Behind the clavicle; joins the other posterior divisions to form the Fasciculus posterior. It is the smallest posterior division.
facts: Posterior divisions carry the fibres for the extensor (posterior) compartments

structures.name: Fasciculus lateralis
structures.origin: Anterior divisions of the Truncus superior and Truncus medius
structures.course: Lies lateral to the 2nd part of the A. axillaris (behind M. pectoralis minor).
facts: Branches: N. pectoralis lateralis, N. musculocutaneus, Radix lateralis n. mediani

structures.name: Fasciculus posterior
structures.course: Lies behind the 2nd part of the A. axillaris.
facts: Branches: N. subscapularis superior, N. thoracodorsalis, N. subscapularis inferior, N. axillaris, N. radialis
Supplies the whole posterior (extensor) side of the upper limb

structures.name: Fasciculus medialis
structures.origin: Anterior division of the Truncus inferior
structures.course: Lies medial to the 2nd part of the A. axillaris.
facts: Branches: N. pectoralis medialis, N. cutaneus brachii medialis, N. cutaneus antebrachii medialis, Radix medialis n. mediani, N. ulnaris

structures.name: Nervus pectoralis lateralis
structures.course: Pierces the Fascia clavipectoralis and reaches the deep surface of M. pectoralis major. A loop to the N. pectoralis medialis (Ansa pectoralis) also brings fibres to M. pectoralis minor.
facts: Named after the cord it comes from – it lies more medial in the chest than the N. pectoralis medialis

structures.name: Nervus subscapularis superior
structures.course: Short nerve that enters the upper part of M. subscapularis.
facts: Supplies the upper part of M. subscapularis
In the Terminologia: one of the Nn. subscapulares

structures.name: Nervus thoracodorsalis
structures.origin: Fasciculus posterior (between the two subscapular nerves)
structures.course: Runs down the posterior axillary wall with the A. thoracodorsalis to the deep surface of M. latissimus dorsi.
facts: Also called the middle subscapular nerve
structures.clinical: At risk during axillary lymph node dissection; the M. latissimus dorsi with this nerve is used as a flap in breast reconstruction.

structures.name: Nervus subscapularis inferior
structures.course: Enters the lower part of M. subscapularis and continues to M. teres major.
facts: Supplies the lower part of M. subscapularis and the whole M. teres major

structures.name: Nervus pectoralis medialis
structures.course: Pierces M. pectoralis minor (supplies it) and ends in the lower, sternocostal part of M. pectoralis major.
facts: Named after the cord it comes from – in the chest it lies lateral to the N. pectoralis lateralis

structures.name: Nervus cutaneus brachii medialis
structures.skin: Skin of the medial side of the upper arm
structures.course: Purely sensory. Runs medial to the V. axillaris and connects with the N. intercostobrachialis (T2).
facts: Smallest branch of the plexus
No muscles – sensory only

structures.name: Nervus cutaneus antebrachii medialis
structures.skin: Skin of the medial side of the forearm (and a small area over the lower medial arm)
structures.course: Purely sensory. Runs with the A. brachialis, pierces the deep fascia with the V. basilica in the middle of the arm.
facts: No muscles – sensory only
structures.clinical: Can be injured during venepuncture or surgery near the V. basilica.

structures.name: Nervus musculocutaneus
structures.skin: Lateral forearm – via its end branch, the N. cutaneus antebrachii lateralis
structures.course: Pierces M. coracobrachialis, runs between M. biceps brachii and M. brachialis and becomes the N. cutaneus antebrachii lateralis at the elbow.
facts: Supplies all three muscles of the anterior compartment of the arm
Memory: BBC – Biceps, Brachialis, Coracobrachialis
structures.clinical: Isolated injury is rare (it is well protected): weak elbow flexion and supination, loss of the biceps reflex, numb lateral forearm.

structures.name: Nervus axillaris
structures.skin: Skin over the lower deltoid ("regimental badge" area) – via the N. cutaneus brachii lateralis superior
structures.course: Passes with the A. circumflexa humeri posterior through the lateral axillary space (Spatium axillare laterale / quadrangular space) and winds around the Collum chirurgicum humeri.
facts: Lateral axillary space = M. teres minor (above), M. teres major (below), Caput longum m. tricipitis (medial), humerus (lateral)
structures.clinical: Injury after dislocation of the shoulder or fracture of the Collum chirurgicum humeri → weak abduction (15–90°) and external rotation, flat shoulder from deltoid atrophy, numb regimental badge area.

structures.name: Nervus radialis
structures.skin: Posterior arm and forearm; radial dorsum of the hand and the first web space (R. superficialis)
structures.course: Runs with the A. profunda brachii in the Sulcus nervi radialis around the humerus, then between M. brachialis and M. brachioradialis. At the elbow it splits into the R. superficialis (sensory) and the R. profundus (motor, continues as N. interosseus antebrachii posterior through M. supinator).
facts: Supplies all extensors of arm and forearm
The R. profundus supplies the extensors of the forearm (from M. extensor carpi radialis brevis and M. supinator on)
structures.clinical: Fracture of the humeral shaft (Sulcus nervi radialis) or "Saturday night palsy" → wrist drop, weak finger extension at the MCP joints, numb first web space. The triceps is usually spared because its branches leave higher. Crutch palsy in the axilla affects the triceps too.

structures.name: Radix lateralis nervi mediani
en: lateral root of the median nerve
structures.course: Joins the Radix medialis in front of the A. axillaris – together they form the "M" (Medianusgabel) with the N. musculocutaneus and the N. ulnaris.
facts: Brings the C6–C7 fibres of the N. medianus (pronator teres, flexor carpi radialis, sensory fibres for the thumb side)

structures.name: Radix medialis nervi mediani
en: medial root of the median nerve
structures.course: Crosses in front of the A. axillaris to join the Radix lateralis – forming the median "M".
facts: Brings the C8–T1 fibres of the N. medianus (long finger flexors, thenar muscles)

structures.name: Nervus medianus
structures.origin: Radix lateralis (Fasciculus lateralis) + Radix medialis (Fasciculus medialis)
muscles: M. flexor digitorum profundus (radial part, digits II–III)
structures.skin: Palmar side of the lateral 3½ fingers and their nail beds; lateral palm
structures.course: No branches in the arm. Runs with the A. brachialis in the Sulcus bicipitalis medialis, enters the forearm between the two heads of M. pronator teres, gives the N. interosseus antebrachii anterior and passes through the Canalis carpi (carpal tunnel).
facts: Hand muscles: LOAF – Lumbricales I–II, Opponens pollicis, Abductor pollicis brevis, Flexor pollicis brevis (superficial head)
FPL, the radial part of FDP and M. pronator quadratus come from the N. interosseus antebrachii anterior
structures.clinical: Carpal tunnel syndrome → tingling in the lateral 3½ fingers (worse at night), thenar atrophy. Lesion at the elbow (supracondylar fracture) → "hand of benediction" when trying to make a fist.

structures.name: Nervus ulnaris
muscles: M. flexor digitorum profundus (ulnar part, digits IV–V)
structures.skin: Palmar and dorsal side of the medial 1½ fingers and the medial hand
structures.course: No branches in the arm. Passes behind the Epicondylus medialis humeri (Sulcus nervi ulnaris – "funny bone"), enters the forearm between the two heads of M. flexor carpi ulnaris and reaches the hand through the Canalis ulnaris (Guyon's canal).
facts: Supplies most of the intrinsic hand muscles
structures.clinical: Injury at the elbow (fracture of the Epicondylus medialis, cubital tunnel) or wrist → claw hand of the ring and little finger, wasting of the Mm. interossei, positive Froment sign, numb little finger.
